1408.title: Buddhist funerals
1408.hook: chanting, merit made for the dead, the seventh- and forty-ninth-day rites
1408.howItsDone: At Buddhist funerals monks or priests chant texts on impermanence, and families make offerings to the monastic community and dedicate the merit to the one who died; in East Asia and Tibet, rites are often held at intervals after the death up to the forty-ninth day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, taking vows as a lay person, and a line in no hurry: someday, maybe.

Monks in saffron sit in a row beside a coffin in a Thai temple. A white cloth is laid across a thread that runs from the coffin to the monks, and they chant in Pali. In a Japanese home, incense curls up before a photograph, and a priest's voice rises and falls through a sutra. In a Tibetan house, a lama reads aloud to someone who has just died, as if the person can still hear. Three different rooms, and underneath, the same two things: the Dhamma spoken aloud, and something good done for the one who has gone. This week begins with Buddhist funerals.
screen: `MONKS CHANTING BESIDE A COFFIN.` → `INCENSE BEFORE A PHOTOGRAPH.` → `A LAMA READING TO THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the chant. At Theravada funerals, the monks may chant a verse that goes back to the Buddha's own passing. In the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, as the Buddha dies, the god Sakka speaks it: impermanent, truly, are all conditioned things; they arise and they pass away; having arisen, they cease; their stilling is happiness. A funeral opens by saying the plain truth out loud. Then, merit for the dead, a cousin of the sharing of merit you met early on. In a short text called the Discourse Outside the Walls, the departed are described standing outside walls, at crossroads, by doorposts, returning to homes once theirs. When relatives give food and drink to the monks and say, may this be for our relatives, the departed are said to share in the goodness and give thanks. Weeping and grief, the text says, do not help the dead. Giving does. So families offer robes and food to the monks and dedicate the merit to the one who died. Then the counting of days. In Tibetan tradition, the text often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead speaks of the in-between state after death lasting up to forty-nine days, and the lama's reading guides the person through it. In China and Japan, tradition holds rites every seventh day until the forty-ninth, when the family gathers again. Across all three rooms, the funeral isn't only for grief. It's something the living still get to do for the dead.
screen: `ALL CONDITIONED THINGS PASS.` · `THE DEPARTED OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · `MERIT GIVEN IN THEIR NAME.` · then, large: `THE SEVENTH AND FORTY-NINTH DAYS.`

segments.voice: This one may be tender; skip it if today isn't the day. Bring to mind one person who has died, their face or their voice; then think of one good thing you've done or could do, and if it feels right, let it rest there: may some of this goodness reach them. If missing someone feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.
Buddhist funerals. Chanting the truth of impermanence, giving in the name of the dead, and marking the days that follow. Today's word.
Your line: merit for the dead. Even a small kindness can be given in someone's name. Gently, until tomorrow.

options: They dedicate the goodness of the gift to the one who died, so the dead can share in it.
It pays the monks for their time, the way you'd pay for any other funeral service.

1409.title: Remembering the dead
1409.howItsDone: Buddhist families in many countries keep a home altar with the names or photographs of their dead beside an image of the Buddha, offering incense, food and light; in East Asia the yearly Obon or Ghost Festival honors ancestors with offerings to the monastic community, lanterns and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhist funerals, and a line about giving: merit for the dead.

A wooden cabinet stands in the corner of a living room in Japan. Behind small doors there's an image of the Buddha, a bell, a little bowl of rice, and thin lacquered tablets with names written on them. Each morning someone opens the doors, lights incense, rings the bell, and sets out fresh rice and tea. The names belong to grandparents and great-grandparents. They're only ink on wood, but they're greeted every morning anyway. A funeral happens once. What comes after can go on for years. Today, remembering the dead.
screen: `A CABINET IN THE LIVING ROOM.` → `NAMES ON LACQUERED TABLETS.` → `GREETED EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Buddhist families keep the dead close in two ways: an altar at home and a day in the year. In Japan it's called a butsudan, a Buddha cabinet, and the names of the family's dead are kept beside the Buddha. In Chinese and Vietnamese homes, ancestor tablets sit on a family altar. The pairing matters. The dead aren't worshipped as gods. They're placed near the Buddha, and offerings are made in the presence of the teaching. Then the day. East Asia has a yearly festival for the dead, called Obon in Japan, which you met earlier on the path, and Yulan or the Ghost Festival in China. Its story comes from the Ullambana Sutra. A disciple of the Buddha, Maudgalyayana, known in the texts for his powers, looks for his dead mother and finds her reborn as a hungry ghost, starving. He offers her a bowl of rice, and it bursts into flame before it reaches her mouth. He runs to the Buddha, who tells him his own power isn't enough. At the end of the rainy-season retreat, he should make offerings to the whole community of monks, for his mother and his ancestors. He does, and in the story his mother is freed. So the yearly rite isn't one person's effort. It's a family, a community, a whole season of practice, pointed at the ones who came before. In Japan, Obon is kept with lanterns and dances that welcome the dead home, then send them off again. Remembering the dead is something done together.
screen: `AN ALTAR AT HOME.` · `NEAR THE BUDDHA, NOT AS GODS.` · `MAUDGALYAYANA AND HIS MOTHER.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it carefully, and bring to mind someone who has died, maybe yesterday's person, maybe someone else, saying their name silently or out loud. Let the small flame keep them company while you breathe; you don't need to say or feel anything in particular. If the loss feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Remembering the dead. A home altar where the names sit near the Buddha, and a yearly rite where a whole community gives in their name. Today's word.
Your line: they are remembered. A name said aloud is one way the dead stay close. Rest well.

what a scholar hears: the Ullambana Sutra's story of Maudgalyayana's mother, behind Obon in Japan and the Yulan festival in China.

worshipping ancestors as gods who answer prayers

chat.meaning: In the butsudan and on ancestor altars, the names of the dead sit beside the Buddha: remembered in the presence of the teaching, not worshipped as gods.

1410.title: The meal chant
1410.hook: the reflection before eating: this food is for health, not for vanity
1410.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks recite a reflection on the purpose of food before eating, drawn from the Buddha's teaching on wise use; Zen communities chant their own meal verses before formal meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering the dead: the home altar, the yearly rite, and Maudgalyayana's mother.

Lunch at a monastery. The bowls are full, the food is warm, and everyone is hungry. Nobody starts eating. Instead, the monks chant a few lines together in Pali, quietly, before the first bite. In a Zen hall the same pause happens with different words and wooden clappers. To a guest it can look strange, sitting in front of good food and not eating it yet. But the pause is the point. Mostly, they're reminding themselves what eating is for. Today, the meal chant.
screen: `FULL BOWLS, NOBODY EATING YET.` → `A FEW LINES CHANTED FIRST.` → `WHAT IS EATING FOR?`

segments.voice: One source is in the Middle Length Discourses, in a teaching on how to let go of what clouds the mind. One of the ways is wise use, and food is one of the things used. The Buddha says a monk reflects wisely as he eats: not for fun, not for intoxication, not for putting on bulk, not for looking good. Only to keep this body going, to ease the pangs of hunger, and to support the holy life. That's the thought behind today's line: for health, not vanity. In Theravada monasteries, a form of these words is still chanted at meals. Notice how unfussy it is. It doesn't say food is bad, or the body is shameful, or eating is a sin. It says eat; just know why. Hunger is real, and food meets it. But food can be pulled into other jobs: showing off, numbing out, comforting yourself after a bad day, turning a meal into a contest. The reflection doesn't scold any of that. It quietly puts food back in its place. Zen communities have their own meal verses, which turn the same idea another way: considering the work that brought this food, and receiving it to support the practice. And then there's the pause itself, one breath before the first bite where you know what you're doing. For the Buddha, eating wisely was one way of guarding the mind. A bowl of rice becomes a small practice at every meal, already built into your life.
screen: `WISE USE OF FOOD.` · `NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.` · `TO KEEP THE BODY GOING.` · then, large: `ONE BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST BITE.`

segments.voice: Notice whether you're hungry right now, without changing it, and picture yourself sitting down to your next meal. Before you pick anything up, say slowly, quietly or in your head, a reflection drawn from the Buddha's words: not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going. Then rest with the breath.
The meal chant. The reflection before eating: this food is to keep the body going and support the practice, not for fun or looks. Today's word.
Your line: for health, not vanity. Food is welcome; the pause just remembers why. Eat well, and see you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: The reflection in the Middle Length Discourses: eat not for fun or looks, but to keep the body going and support the holy life. Food isn't bad; just know why.

1411.title: Plan your retreat
1411.hook: a day, a weekend or ten days: plan one for this coming year
1411.howItsDone: Buddhists go on retreats of a day, a weekend or longer at monasteries and meditation centers; monks keep the vassa, the rains retreat, and lay people may join it on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meal chant: not for fun, not for looks, only to keep this body going.

Once, the Buddha told his monks he wanted to go into seclusion for three months, and that no one should come to him except the one who brought his alms food. The monks agreed. Three months went by. When he came out, he told them how he had spent most of that time: mindful of the breath, in and out. The teacher of the whole community took time away. He planned it, he told people, and he came back and said what he did there. That's a retreat. Today, with the year's practice traditions nearly done, plan your retreat.
screen: `THE BUDDHA GOES INTO SECLUSION.` → `ONLY THE ONE WHO BRINGS FOOD.` → `HE COMES BACK AND TELLS THEM.`

segments.voice: That story is in the Connected Discourses, in the chapter on breathing. It gives a retreat its shape: a set time, a protected space, a plain practice, and a return. Retreat is woven through Buddhist life. The monks' rains retreat, the vassa, began in the Vinaya with a simple rule: during the rainy season, stay put in one place. Tradition makes that season a stretch of deeper practice, and lay people may join in, coming to the monastery on moon days. Earlier on this path you met what a retreat is, and sesshin, the Zen week of silence. In some meditation centers today, people sit for ten days in silence. But a retreat doesn't have to be long. A day of mindfulness at home counts. So does a weekend at a monastery that welcomes guests. What makes it a retreat isn't the length. It's the four things from the Buddha's three months: a time you decide on in advance, a space protected from ordinary demands, one plain practice, and a way back. The planning isn't a chore before the real thing. In the Buddha's story, telling the monks was part of it: someone knew where he was and who would bring the food. The practices of these past weeks, chanting, bowing, pilgrimage, the perfections, the moon days, all live more deeply on a retreat. So today's step is small and practical. Not go now. Just know: when, where, how long, and who will know.
screen: `THE BUDDHA'S THREE MONTHS AWAY.` · `VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.` · `A DAY, A WEEKEND OR TEN DAYS.` · then, large: `WHEN, WHERE, HOW LONG, WHO KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit for a few breaths the way the Buddha spent his three months: just the breath, in and out. Then let a plan take shape: when you could step away this year, a Saturday, a long weekend, ten days; where, your own room with the phone off, a nearby temple, a center that runs retreats; what one practice you'd keep there, and who you'd tell. Hold the four answers lightly, as if in pencil.
Plan your retreat. A set time, a protected place, one plain practice and a way back, decided before you go, as the Buddha did. Today's word.
Your line: plan it. Even a single Saturday counts. I'll be here tomorrow.

1412.title: Practice traditions, closed
1412.hook: chant, bow, retreat, pilgrimage, perfections, vows
1412.howItsDone: Buddhists in different schools keep practices such as chanting, bowing, meditation retreats, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows, and some settle on one or two that they keep daily, often with a teacher's guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, plan your retreat: a set time, a protected place, one practice, and a way back.

Lay these past weeks out on a table like objects from a long trip. A chant sheet in Pali. A page of the Heart Sutra, marked for a wooden drum. The mani, sung. The name of Amitabha, walked around a hall. A bow, from a small nod to the full length of the floor. A long retreat in noble silence, and a sesshin with sore legs and tea at the end. A map of pilgrim roads: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, the island of temples, the mountain. The perfections, one a day. Moon days. Vows for others. A funeral chant, a memorial altar, a meal chant, and yesterday's plan. That's a lot to carry home. Today's step is small and honest: pick up one thing from the table.
screen: `CHANT, BOW, RETREAT.` → `PILGRIMAGE, PERFECTIONS, VOWS.` → `PICK UP ONE THING.`

segments.voice: The tradition has a word for all of this: bhavana. It's often translated meditation, but it's wider than sitting. It means cultivation, bringing something into being, the way a gardener brings up a plant. Chanting is bhavana. So is bowing, giving, keeping a precept on a moon day. Every practice here is a different kind of gardening. Why one and not all? The Dhammapada has a picture for how good grows, in Max Müller's words: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about not thinking little of small good acts. A drop doesn't fill a pot. A drop, again and again, does. A month of tasting is a sampler. One practice, kept, fills the pot. How to choose? Some teachers put it simply: start with what you'll actually do. Not the most impressive practice; the one that fits your mornings, your body, your house. A short chant you can say while the kettle boils may grow further than a ten-day retreat you never book. And the schools don't ask you to pick a team. These weeks, a Theravada chant sat next to a Zen drum and a Pure Land name, each taught on its own terms. Choosing one to deepen isn't a verdict on the others. It's just where your water-drops land for now. And from tomorrow, the festival year comes round again, starting with the full moon of Vesak.
screen: `BHAVANA: BRINGING INTO BEING.` · `A DROP, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `START WITH WHAT YOU'LL DO.` · then, large: `CHOOSE ONE.`

segments.voice: Let the practices pass slowly through your mind: the chant, the bow, the retreat, the pilgrim road, the perfections, the vows. Don't decide with your head; notice which one your attention leans toward, the way a plant leans toward a window, and when one stays, picture doing it tomorrow for a few minutes, in your real kitchen or your real chair. If more than one comes, keep the first.
Practice traditions. Ways Buddhists of different schools cultivate the path: chanting, bowing, retreat, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows. Today's word.
Your line: choose one. The others will wait for you, too. On to the festivals.

1413.title: Vesak, the fourth time
1413.hook: Vesak as the schools keep it, side by side
1413.howItsDone: In Theravada countries, Buddhists keep Vesak on a full moon with temple visits, extra precepts, giving and lamps; in Japan, Korea and China the birth is often kept as its own day, and in Tibet the month of Saga Dawa is set apart.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the practice traditions with one simple, honest line: choose one.

Four scenes, all honoring one person. In a Sri Lankan town, a lit gateway the height of a house shows a story from the Buddha's past lives, and a stall hands out free drinks. In a Japanese temple courtyard, children ladle sweet tea over a tiny statue of a baby with one hand pointing up. In Seoul, a river of paper lotus lanterns moves through the streets at night. In Lhasa, pilgrims walk the circuit around the old city all month long, prayer wheels turning. Different dates, different food, different music. This is your fourth Vesak on the path, so today, instead of standing in one country, stand where you can see them all at once.
screen: `GATEWAYS AND FREE DRINKS.` → `SWEET TEA OVER A BABY.` → `LANTERNS AND A HOLY MONTH.`

segments.voice: Start with Vesak as Theravada lands like Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar keep it: one full moon remembers three things together, the Buddha's birth, his awakening and his passing away. That's your line today: born, awake, gone. Next, the schools that separate them. In Japan, the birth stands on its own, at the flower festival in spring, with the sweet tea and the pointing baby. The awakening has its own day in winter, and the passing its own day too. Korean and Chinese communities also keep the birthday as its own feast, with lanterns and the bathing of a small Buddha statue. Then Tibet, where a whole month, Saga Dawa, is set apart. Its full moon remembers the awakening and the passing, and in some tellings the birth as well. Some Tibetan teachers say that good and harmful actions done in that month carry extra weight. Now set them side by side. The dates differ, the music differs, but underneath, the same thing is said. The Dhammapada has a short verse for it, in Max Müller's words: "Happy is the arising of the awakened." Each school, in its own way, is glad that this person was born, woke up, and taught. And a festival kept side by side isn't a contest over who keeps it best. A lantern in Seoul and a lamp in Colombo are both lit for the same arrival.
screen: `ONE MOON, THREE EVENTS.` · `SEPARATE DAYS IN JAPAN.` · `A HOLY MONTH IN TIBET.` · then, large: `HAPPY IS THE ARISING.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it safely where you can see it; a phone screen turned low, or the light in the window, will do. For a few breaths think born, a small life arriving; for a few more, awake, eyes open; for a few more, gone, a flame that will one day go out. Then let the words fall away and just watch the light.
Vesak. The full moon on which Theravada Buddhists remember the birth, the awakening and the passing, kept in different ways by different schools. Today's word.
Your line: born, awake, gone. Three events, one full moon, and many lanterns lit. Happy Vesak.

1414.title: Poson again
1414.howItsDone: On Poson, Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Mahinda's arrival with pilgrimages to Mihintale and Anuradhapura, temple visits, extra precepts, and free food and drink stalls along the roads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vesak side by side: lanterns, sweet tea, a holy month, and one line: born, awake, gone.

Footprints in soft ground at the edge of a forest. Big ones. A tracker kneels beside them. A beginner would stand up and say: a huge bull elephant came through here. The skilled tracker doesn't, not yet. He follows. That picture comes from a sermon, and by the Sri Lankan chronicle's telling, it's the sermon a monk named Mahinda gave to a king on a mountain, on the day the teaching reached the island. You've met the king and the mango tree riddle before. Today, on Poson's full moon, follow the footprints instead.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS AT THE FOREST EDGE.` → `THE SKILLED TRACKER WAITS.` → `THE SERMON ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: The chronicle names the sermon: the shorter discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint, in the Middle Length Discourses. In it, the tracker knows that some small elephants leave big prints. So he follows the trail, past scrapes on the trees, past broken branches, until he sees the great elephant itself, and only then says: this is it. The discourse lays out the path one step after another: hearing the teaching, taking up a simple life, keeping the precepts, guarding the senses, sitting. Each step is a footprint. A careful follower, it says, doesn't jump to the end; confidence grows as the trail is walked. Why would a monk choose this for a king meeting the teaching for the first time? It doesn't ask him to swallow anything whole. It says: here's a trail, follow it, and see. Then the people on the trail. The chronicle remembers Mahinda as the son of the emperor Ashoka, and his sister Sanghamitta as the nun who brought a cutting of the bodhi tree. Poson honors them, and a simple fact: a teaching never arrives by itself. Somebody carries it. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's words: "The gift of the law exceeds all gifts." On Poson, pilgrims in white climb the steps at Mihintale to the place where tradition says that gift was handed over. This week, too, a funeral chant, names on a home altar, a meal chant and a Vesak lamp each reached you because somebody carried it.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT'S FOOTPRINT.` · `FOLLOW THE TRAIL, STEP BY STEP.` · `SOMEBODY CARRIES IT.` · then, large: `WHO BROUGHT IT.`

segments.voice: Walk the trail backward: how did this path reach you? A book on a shelf, a friend who meditates, a grandparent's shrine, a teacher, a stranger's offhand remark, a podcast at midnight; let one person or one moment come to mind and, if you'd like, silently say: thank you for bringing it. You don't need to know whether they'd call themselves Buddhist.
Poson. A full moon in Sri Lanka, remembering the day the teaching reached the island, carried by Mahinda. Today's word.
Your line: who brought it. Thanks can travel back down the trail, too. Go gently.
